summary: Itamar Friedman, CEO and co-founder of Qodo (formerly CodiumAI), delivers a talk on "vibe coding with confidence" at the AI Engineer World's Fair, soft-launching a new CLI tool. He frames the evolution of AI developer tools across three generations: Gen 1.0 was autocomplete in IDEs, which required existing developer skill; Gen 2.0 brought agentic chat that let even juniors generate more code but created review burdens for seniors; and Gen 3.0 will involve CLI-based commands directing agents through end-to-end SDLC workflows as if they were team members. Friedman argues that while developers like current AI tools, none has been a true gamechanger yet, particularly for enterprise developers on existing large codebases. He differentiates between "noobs" who benefit from prompt-to-software generation and enterprise developers who need reliable, versatile workflows covering bug fixing, refactoring, feature changes, testing, and code review. Friedman visualizes software development as a V-shape (planning→code→tests→review) and argues the gamechanger is compressing this V by connecting workflows and agents via MCP and A2A protocols, analogous to how Wiz built a holistic cloud security platform. He references Karpathy's walk-back of vibe coding for professional code and notes AI tools are far less effective on large existing codebases versus greenfield work. Friedman then demonstrates Qodo's multi-agent architecture, including a deep-ask agent, the Qodo Merge code review tool, and an open-source coverage agent. The CLI tool lets developers chat, call specialized agents, create new agents on the fly, pipe agents and workflows together, and connect to pre-commit/post-commit hooks. He shows creating a review agent that initializes MCP, searches capabilities, and generates agent definitions with instructions, tools, and output schemas. Friedman notes A2A is not yet adopted—no speakers at the event used it—but envisions parallel agents with discoverability and handshakes. He highlights that CLI can auto-generate flexible interfaces (like a code review UI) fitting the task, referencing Simon Willison's CLI-centric demo. He closes predicting a future of swarms of specialized agents with different credentials and best practices, arriving in 2025-2026.

sections.title: Introduction and CLI Soft Launch
sections.summary: Itamar Friedman introduces himself as CEO/co-founder of Qodo and announces a soft launch of their CLI tool. He polls the audience on usage of Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Aider, setting up the theme of why CLI matters for vibe coding with confidence.

sections.title: AI Developer Tool Evolution: Gen 1.0 to Gen 3.0
sections.summary: Friedman traces three generations of AI developer tools: Gen 1.0 autocomplete, Gen 2.0 agentic chat, and an emerging Gen 3.0 where developers use CLI to command agents through end-to-end flows as team members. He argues current tools are liked but not yet gamechangers.

sections.title: Noobs vs Enterprise and AI Across the SDLC
sections.summary: Friedman differentiates noobs (who want prompt-to-software) from enterprise developers (who need reliable, versatile workflows across the SDLC). He argues vibe coding focused only on writing code fast is insufficient for heavy-duty software, which also needs bug fixing, refactoring, testing, and review. He proposes shift-left review and testing as a semi-gamechanger.

sections.title: V-Shape Development and the Gamechanger via Connected Agents
sections.summary: Friedman visualizes software development as a V-shape on axes of time and executability (planning→code→tests→review). The gamechanger is compressing this V by having different workflows and agents communicate via MCP and A2A, creating a holistic solution for intelligent software development—paralleling how Wiz consolidated cloud security.

sections.title: Vibe Coding with Confidence: Karpathy's Evolution and Greenfield vs Enterprise
sections.summary: Friedman discusses Karpathy's walk-back of vibe coding for code he professionally cares about, noting Karpathy now emphasizes context and structured workflows. He cites an opinion leader noting AI coding tools are far less useful on existing large codebases than greenfield work, setting up the enterprise challenge.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Architecture and CLI Tool Capabilities
sections.summary: Friedman describes Qodo's multi-agent architecture: a deep-ask agent for code research, Qodo Merge for code review (collecting best practices over time), and IDE-integrated tools for shift-left context. He announces the CLI tool release and demonstrates chatting with it, calling specialized agents like the explain agent, and creating new agents on the fly.

sections.title: Piping Agents, A2A, and Agent Definitions
sections.summary: Friedman demonstrates piping agents together in CLI (code generation→coverage→review), notes this is not yet A2A but a pipeline passing results. He envisions a CLI command for A2A enabling parallel agents with discoverability and handshakes. He shows the generated review agent's definition with instructions, tools, and output schema, noting no speakers at the event use A2A yet.

sections.title: Flexible IDEs from CLI and Swarm of Agents Future
sections.summary: Friedman notes CLI can use organizational best practices and success/failure criteria for confident coding, and connect to pre-commit/post-commit hooks. Referencing Simon Willison's demo, he highlights that CLI can auto-generate flexible interfaces fitting the task (e.g., a code review UI), making fixed IDEs less relevant. He closes predicting a future of swarms of specialized agents with different credentials and best practices, arriving in 2025-2026.
